planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade; Mikinori's epimedium is a Chinese woodland species named for plant collector Mikinori Ogisu, notable for its unusually variable flower color.

directions: Mikinori's epimedium is a Chinese woodland species from the Enshi area of Hubei Province, named to honor the Japanese plant collector Mikinori Ogisu, whose fieldwork in western China brought many now-cultivated Epimedium species into horticulture. Wild populations and cultivated collections show real variation in flower color, rhizome type, and leaf indumentum from plant to plant. As with other clump- to slowly-spreading Chinese epimediums, it bears typical arrow-shaped compound leaflets and airy sprays of small spurred flowers held above the foliage in spring. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge, and provide the reliably moist, humus-rich woodland conditions this species experiences in its native limestone-associated habitat.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil in dappled shade to full shade; a slowly spreading evergreen species from eastern Sichuan Province with narrow, burgundy-mottled foliage and distinctively shaped flowers.

directions: Native to eastern Sichuan Province, China, this species tolerates alkaline soils better than many epimediums. It is a slowly spreading, evergreen species valued for its narrow, medium-sized arrow-shaped leaflets, which emerge heavily mottled with burgundy in spring and mature to a handsome dark green. Its small but distinctively shaped flowers have reflexed, pure white inner sepals set off against rose-red petals with short, strongly curved spurs, held in a manner unlike the larger, showier blooms of many garden epimedium hybrids. Once established, the wiry rhizomes are notably drought tolerant, allowing this species to persist in the dry, root-filled soil under mature deciduous trees where few other groundcovers thrive. Trim old foliage back in late winter to display the spring flower display fully.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; an evergreen, few-flowered western Sichuan species bearing short flower stalks of large, bright cream-yellow blooms above bold evergreen foliage.

directions: Native to western Sichuan Province, China, this species is named in honor of Chinese botanist Wen-pei Fang, who documented much of the region's flora, and was among the notable Epimedium discoveries introduced to Western horticulture by plant collector Mikinori Ogisu. This evergreen species is few-flowered but showy, producing short flowering stalks topped with relatively large, bright cream to yellow blooms above bold, leathery evergreen leaflets. Its clean yellow flower color and evergreen habit have made it a valued parent in hybridizing, most notably crossed with E. acuminatum to produce the garden hybrid E. x omeiense. Grow in the same humus-rich, evenly drained woodland conditions favored by other Sichuan epimediums, and remove tattered old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; an evergreen, clump-forming species from northwestern and central China bearing large airy panicles of small starry flowers.

directions: A long-cultivated, evergreen, clump-forming species native to northwestern and central China. Hardier collections from Shaanxi Province have proven reliable into zone 5, forming a leafy clump with flowering panicles rising above it. Its medium-sized evergreen leaflets have spiny margins and emerge flecked with crimson before maturing to glossy dark green, providing good winter interest. In spring it produces unusually large, airy panicles of small starry flowers, each with narrow, white, reflexed inner sepals and tiny orange-yellow spurred petals, a more floriferous, finer-textured display than many larger-flowered epimediums. It tolerates dry shade well once established and is among the more heat-tolerant Chinese species. Groom by removing old foliage in late winter to showcase the flowering display.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade; a selected clone of the natural hybrid E. x omeiense collected on Mount Emei in Sichuan, with cherry-red inner sepals and bright orange-and-yellow spurs.

directions: Akame (a Japanese name meaning red bud) is a selected clone of the naturally occurring hybrid Epimedium x omeiense, a cross between E. acuminatum and E. fangii found on Mount Emei (Omei Shan) in Sichuan, China, and introduced to cultivation by plant collector Mikinori Ogisu. It is a large, bold, evergreen epimedium with glossy, dark, sagittate leaves that often turn maroon in fall. In early spring it produces open sprays of brilliant flowers with cherry-red inner sepals and bright orange-and-yellow spurs, the cup most intensely colored and rimmed in yellow, among the most vividly colored blooms in the genus. Once established it tolerates dry shade, though it performs best with consistent moisture and rich woodland soil. Cut back old foliage in late winter to fully display the spring flower show.

common_name: Hubei Treasure Epimedium (Large-Flowered Pink Mottled Epimedium)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; a wild-collected selection of E. leptorrhizum with notably larger flowers than the species, on an evergreen, rhizome-spreading plant.

directions: Hubei Treasure is a distinctive wild-collected clone of the species mottled epimedium (Epimedium leptorrhizum), found growing in the cracks of a cliff along the Sichuan/Hubei provincial border in China. It shares the species' slender, wide-running rhizomes and fast-spreading groundcover habit, but produces notably larger flowers than typical wild plants: near-white spurs backed by rich, saturated pink inner sepals, a striking departure from the paler lavender-pink of the wild species, along with larger evergreen leaves. As with the species, it spreads readily to form an attractive, weed-suppressing mat in dry shade under trees once established. Cut back old foliage in late winter to display the spring flowers, and provide humus-rich soil with reliable moisture during the growing season for best performance.

common_name: Rose Queen Epimedium (RHS AGM Rose-Pink Longspur Barrenwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; a classic, RHS Award of Garden Merit longspur epimedium with bronze young foliage and sprays of rose-pink flowers with long white spurs.

directions: Rose Queen is one of the oldest and most widely grown cultivars of the Japanese and Korean species Epimedium grandiflorum, and a longtime holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Compound leaves emerge bronze-tinted in spring before maturing to green, providing an attractive backdrop for the wiry flower stems that rise above the foliage in mid-spring, carrying open sprays of bright rose-pink flowers with long, elegant white spurs. Like other longspur epimediums, it is a superb, drought-tolerant groundcover for dry shade beneath deciduous trees, forming a dense, weed-suppressing carpet over time. Cut back old foliage in late winter to fully reveal the spring flower display, and divide congested clumps in fall to propagate or rejuvenate plantings.

common_name: White Queen Epimedium (RHS AGM Pure White Longspur Barrenwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; a classic, RHS Award of Garden Merit longspur epimedium with coppery-tinted young foliage and masses of pure white, long-spurred flowers.

directions: White Queen is a long-established cultivar of the Japanese and Korean species Epimedium grandiflorum and a companion selection to the pink-flowered Rose Queen, both holders of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Divided leaves are flushed coppery-red as they emerge in spring, setting off masses of large, pure white, long-spurred flowers that bloom in airy sprays just below the foliage canopy in mid-spring. As with other forms of this species, it is a tough, drought-tolerant groundcover once established, thriving in the dry, root-filled soil beneath mature deciduous trees where it forms a dense weed-suppressing mat. Cut back old foliage in late winter before flowering to display the blooms fully, and divide crowded clumps in fall to propagate new plants.
